name: Julius Caesar
role: Roman general, consul and dictator (c. 100-44 BC)
summary: A Roman politician from the populares tradition who conquered Gaul, defeated Pompey and the Senate's forces in a civil war, and ruled as dictator until his assassination. He pushed land grants for the poor and veterans, relieved some debt and published the Senate's proceedings, extended citizenship, and pardoned many opponents. His surviving record shows little stated political theory, so most statements about modern institutions have no recorded position.

strong-leader.rationale: As consul in 59 BC he pushed his agrarian law through over his colleague's omens, and he accepted the dictatorship for life, ruling with little reference to the Senate.

widespread-small-property.rationale: He distributed public land to many small holders and settled veterans on land without dispossessing owners; colonies were also planted for his soldiers.

political-violence-never.rationale: He justified marching his army into Italy in 49 BC as defence of his rights and the tribunes (Civil War 1.7), while also offering mutual disarmament; he held armed action justified here.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He conquered Gaul, crossed the Rhine, invaded Britain and imposed tribute (stated in his Commentaries), and planned wars against Dacia and Parthia for the 'extension of the Empire'.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Nulled on re-check: the earlier 0 mixed his reported speech on the Catilinarians (Sallust's composition) with Civil War complaints about the Senate's emergency decree; no single act or own statement settles whether he accepts suspending ordinary protections.

reviewHistory.rationale: In the Catilinarian debate (as written by Sallust) he opposed executing citizens outside the laws; in the Civil War he accepted the Senate's emergency decree only for real unrest and objected to its use against the tribunes. Points both ways.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: He gave Roman citizenship to 'all who practised medicine at Rome, and all teachers of the liberal arts, to make them more desirous of living in the city and to induce others to resort to it' (Suetonius, Divus Julius 42.1), with no period of residence required.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: No recorded position on re-election limits; taking the dictatorship for life is something nearby.

death-penalty.rationale: He had the pirates who held him captive crucified (Suetonius) and had the Veneti's senate put to death and the rest sold into slavery (Gallic War III.16).

reviewHistory.rationale: In Sallust's version of his speech he opposed executing the Catilinarian conspirators, calling death a relief, and proposed life custody, but he did not oppose the penalty in law; he also crucified pirates and executed the Veneti senate.

sacred-ruler.rationale: In his eulogy of his aunt Julia he claimed for his family the 'sanctity of kings' and kinship to the gods through Venus; later he accepted honours beyond those of mortals.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Suetonius reports (via Titus Ampius, a hostile witness) that he said men should regard his word as law, and that he named magistrates years ahead with disregard of law and precedent; contested evidence.

leader-cult.rationale: He accepted statues among those of the kings, temples and altars, a special priest and a month named for him, per Suetonius.

land-redistribution.rationale: His agrarian law gave state-owned land to the poor and to veterans, but he avoided taking land from private owners for veteran settlements, so the evidence points both ways.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He enrolled additional patrician families, creating hereditary rank rather than ending it; he did not discuss abolition.

native-born-offices.rationale: He gave citizenship to many provincials and admitted some Gauls to the Senate.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: As consul in 59 BC he divided the Campanian public land, without casting lots, 'among twenty thousand citizens who had three or more children each' (Suetonius, Divus Julius 20.3).

reviewHistory.rationale: As consul he divided public land in Campania among 20,000 citizens who had three or more children, and as dictator he restricted emigration to keep up Rome's population; he also granted citizenship to attract doctors and teachers.

non-intervention.rationale: He justified entering Gaul by the Senate's charge to protect the Aedui, and in Egypt settled the royal dispute as 'common friend and arbitrator' of the Roman people.

suppress-opposition.rationale: His acts point both ways: as consul in 59 BC he had Cato dragged from the Senate to prison and frightened Lucullus into silence, and in the civil war he treated the neutral as friends, spared his opponents at Pharsalus and pardoned those he had not yet pardoned (Suetonius, Divus Julius 20.4, 75).

open-government-data.rationale: His first act as consul in 59 BC was that proceedings of the Senate and people be compiled and published each day.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: His Commentaries justify the Gallic campaigns as defence of allies, but he crossed the Rhine and invaded Britain unprovoked and planned Parthian and Dacian wars; his stated framing is defensive, so contested.

notes:
His clemency to defeated opponents (Corfinium, Pharsalus) is documented in his Commentaries and Suetonius but matched no statement closely. Speeches reported by Sallust are a historian's composition and held to low confidence. Debt relief, the Julian calendar, sumptuary laws and the reduced grain roll were considered but did not match a statement's wording.

Later pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-11-14): brought to rules 7. Read Caesar's own letter to Cicero as preserved in Cicero's letters to Atticus (Gutenberg 50692, Loeb translation) for suppress-opposition 0 low (acts point both ways: Cato and Lucullus in 59 BC, clemency after Pharsalus); Suetonius (Divus Julius 20, 42, 75) for pronatalist-incentives (0 low to +1 medium: Campanian land to 20,000 citizens with three or more children) and long-naturalization-wait (-2 medium: citizenship for doctors and teachers settling in Rome); Parenti's popular history was used only as a lead to the ancient texts; death-penalty re-answered from acts (+1 medium); emergency-suspend-protections nulled (the 0 mixed words with acts).
